4628               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
4629               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
4630               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.

4632               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
4633               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
4634               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
4635               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
4636               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.

4766               	;
4767               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
4768               	; 	'
4769               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4770               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4771               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4772               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4773               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4774               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4775               	; 	'
4776               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4777               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4778               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4779               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4780               	; 	'
4781               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
4782               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
4783               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page

5491               	;
5492               	; 	' ======================================================================
5493               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5494               	; 	' ======================================================================
5495               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5496               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5497               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5498               	; 	' of running.
5499               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5500               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5501               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5502               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5503               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5504               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5505               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5506               	; 	'
5507               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5508               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5509               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5510               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5511               	; 	'
5512               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5513               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5514               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5515               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5516               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5517               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5518               	; 	'
5519               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5520               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5521               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5522               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5523               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5524               	; 	'
5525               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5526               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5527               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5528               	; draw_screen:
5529               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN
5530               	; 	#if NES
5531               	; 	' AND BLACK BACK FOR THE STORE -- see the note in title_draw. Index 0 is
5532               	; 	' the universal backdrop, so the dark blue the title sets would otherwise
5533               	; 	' tint every outline, the HUD row and the ground under the scanner.
5534               	; 	'
5535               	; 	' A DARK BLUE BACKDROP WAS TRIED HERE, to give the sunset a fourth band
5536               	; 	' (see nes_inkmap in assets/nes_chr.asm). It works, and it costs the
5537               	; 	' escalator, the radar ground and every black outline in the store, all of
5538               	; 	' which ride on index 0. One sky band is not worth the store's line work.
5539               	; 	PALETTE 0,15			' black

5600               	; 		#if NES
5601               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5602               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5603               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5604               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5605               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5606               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5607               	; 		'
5608               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5609               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5610               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5611               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5612               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5613               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5614               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5615               	; 		'
5616               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5617               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.
5618               	; 		SCREEN stor_tpl,#dsrc,#ddst,32,3,32

5676               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5677               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top
5678               	; 	' pixel sits under the slab row of the band ABOVE -- and a slab row is
5679               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped
5680               	; 	' three pixels short of the bar on every storey. It read as a beam that
5681               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.
5682               	; 	'
5683               	; 	' It cannot be drawn into either template. The beam belongs to the band
5684               	; 	' below and the row belongs to the band above, and the two templates are
5685               	; 	' chosen independently per screen, so no template knows both. So the
5686               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a
5687               	; 	' per-template column table -- the same shape as the escalator's head cap.
5688               	; 	'
5689               	; 	' Bands 0 and 1 only. Band 2's top row is the ROOF DECK, which is grey
5690               	; 	' over grey with no green to bridge, and the roof itself has no band
5691               	; 	' above it at all.
5692               	; 	' BANDS 0 TO 2 -- ALL THREE SHOPPING FLOORS. It used to stop at 1,
5693               	; 	' because band 2's ceiling is the ROOF DECK and the deck had no green

6338               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between

6340               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it

6347               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64

6467               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6468               	; 			'
6469               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6470               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6471               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6472               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6473               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6474               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6475               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6476               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6477               	; 			'
6478               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6479               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6480               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6481               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6482               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6483               	; 			'
6484               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6485               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6486               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6487               	; 			'
6488               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6489               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6490               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6491               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6492               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6493               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
6494               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
6495               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every
6496               	; 			' ball has it computed below. It was seeded here from a
6497               	; 			' table byte that no longer exists, and for anything but
6498               	; 			' a ball that seed was never read.

7808               	; 	' walked on to x = 254, the crossing routine then noticed there was no

8964               	;
8965               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8966               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8967               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8968               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8969               	; 	'
8970               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8971               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8972               	; 	'
8973               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8974               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8975               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8976               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8977               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8978               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8979               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8980               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8981               	; 	' merged object.
8982               	; 	'
8983               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
8984               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
8985               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
8986               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
8987               	; 	'
8988               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
8989               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
8990               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
8991               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
8992               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
8993               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
8994               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
8995               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
8996               	; 	'
8997               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
8998               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
8999               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
9000               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
9001               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
9002               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
9003               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
9004               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
9005               	; 	' its bottom half together.
9006               	; 	'
9007               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
9008               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
9009               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
9010               	; 	#if NES
9011               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
9012               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
9013               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
9014               	; 	'
9015               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
9016               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
9017               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
9018               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
9019               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
9020               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
9021               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
9022               	; 	'
9023               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
9024               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
9025               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
9026               	; 	'
9027               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
9028               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
9029               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
9030               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
9031               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
9032               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
9033               	; 	'                   the whole time.
9034               	; 	'
9035               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
9036               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
9037               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
9038               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
9039               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
9040               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
9041               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
9042               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
9043               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
9044               	; 	'
9045               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
9046               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
9047               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
9048               	; 	' they only need setting once.
9049               	; 	'
9050               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
9051               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
9052               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
9053               	; 	' as him changing pose.
9054               	; nes_swp16:
9055               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
9056               	; 	'
9057               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
9058               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
9059               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
9060               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
9061               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
9062               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
9063               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
9064               	; 	'
9065               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
9066               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
9067               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
9068               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
9069               	; 	'
9070               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
9071               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
9072               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
9073               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
9074               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
9075               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
9076               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
9077               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
9078               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
9079               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
9080               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
9081               	; 	ntab = 0
9082               	; 	#ncol = 0
9083               	; 	nink = 1
9084               	; 	ncnt = 4
9085               	; 	WAIT
9086               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9087               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
9088               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9089               	; 	WAIT
9090               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9091               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9092               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9093               	; 	WAIT
9094               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9095               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9096               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9097               	; 	WAIT
9098               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9099               	; 	RETURN
9100               	;
9101               	; nes_def:
9102               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9103               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9104               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9105               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9106               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9107               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9108               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9109               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
9110               	; 	RETURN
9111               	;
9112               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
9113               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9114               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9115               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9116               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9117               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9118               	; 	'
9119               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
9120               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
9121               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
9122               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9123               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9124               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9125               	; 	'
9126               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9127               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9128               	; nes_escd:
9129               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
9130               	; 	RETURN
9131               	;
9132               	; nes_tpl:
9133               	; 	nti = lv8(nbl)
9134               	; 	nti = nti + klsc
9135               	; 	#ntb = #stix + nti
9136               	; 	ntd = PEEK(#ntb)
9137               	; 	#ntc = #tsrc(ntd)
9138               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #nta
9139               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #sttp
9140               	; 	ntv = PEEK(#ntc)
9141               	; 	RETURN
9142               	; 	#endif

9225               	; 	' A PILLAR'S CAP MAY BE CLEARED; AN END WALL'S MAY NOT. beam_one stamps

9227               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize

9233               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above

9235               	; 	' nothing.
9236               	; 	'

9238               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9239               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9240               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no

9248               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.

9875               	; upd_obst:
9876               cvb_UPD_OBST
9877               	; 	' ONE ACCUMULATOR PER KIND, NOT PER SLOT. Every hazard of a kind moves at
9878               	; 	' that kind's speed, so three calls a pass serve all eight slots.
9879               	; 	'
9880               	; 	' Per-slot would have meant up to eight calls of O(fdv) work every pass --
9881               	; 	' the positive feedback loop CLAUDE.md 3A warns about, where a slow pass is
9882               	; 	' made slower by the very code meant to take the loop rate out of the
9883               	; 	' game's behaviour. It also saves the eight bytes an obacc() would cost,
9884               	; 	' and ColecoVision RAM is the tighter budget.
9885               	; 	pacc = oacb
9886 D532 D820  54 	movb @cvb_OACB,@cvb_PACC
     D534 20D1     
     D536 2130     
9887               	; 	psp64 = obsp

     D53A 214F     
     D53C 2138

     D540 A980

10175               	;
10176               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10177               	; 	'
10178               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10179               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10180               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10181               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10182               	; 	'
10183               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10184               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10185               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10186               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10187               	; 	'
10188               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
10189               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
10190               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
10191               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
10192               	; 	'
10193               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10194               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10195               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10196               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10197               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10198               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.
10199               	; pace_step:

10687               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10688               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10689               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10690               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10691               	; 	' runs every pass.
10692               	; 	'
10693               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10694               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10695               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10696               	; 	'
10697               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10698               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10699               	; 	'
10700               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10701               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10702               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10703               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10704               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10705               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10706               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10707               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10708               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10709               	; 	'
10710               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10711               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10712               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10713               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10714               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10715               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10716               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10717               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10718               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10719               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10720               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
10721               	; 	' flight looking busy.
10722               	; 	'
10723               	; 	' TWO THINGS END THE RUN, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE ON SCREEN.

10818               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10819               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10820               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10821               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10822               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10823               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10824               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10825               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10826               	; 	'
10827               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10828               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10829               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10830               	; 	'
10831               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10832               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10833               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10834               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10835               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10836               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10837               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10838               	; 	'
10839               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10840               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10841               	; 	'
10842               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10843               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10844               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10845               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10846               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10847               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10848               	; 	'
10849               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10850               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10851               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10852               	; 	' before any of this.
10853               	; 	'
10854               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10855               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10856               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10857               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10858               	; 	' journey.

10860               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels

11323               	;
11324               	; 	' ======================================================================
11325               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11326               	; 	' ======================================================================
11327               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11328               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11329               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11330               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11331               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11332               	; 	'
11333               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11334               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11335               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11336               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11337               	; 	' broken.
11338               	; 	'
11339               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11340               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11341               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11342               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11343               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11344               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.
11345               	; 	'
11346               	; 	' So obht() is a countdown, not a flag. A hit sets it to HITREF; it ticks
11347               	; 	' down only while the player is CLEAR, and the same obstacle cannot charge
11348               	; 	' again until it reaches zero. Contact holds the count up, so parking
11349               	; 	' inside something never earns a second penalty either.
11350               	; coll_obst:
11351               cvb_COLL_OBST
11352               	; 	IF klst = ST_ESC THEN RETURN		' riding is invincible, per the
11353 DF3E D020  34 	movb @cvb_KLST,r0
     DF40 21C0     
11354 DF42 0201  20 	li r1,768   ; 3*256
     DF44 0300     
11355 DF46 9001  18 	cb r1,r0
11356 DF48 1302  14 	jeq cv657
11357 DF4A 0460  28 	b @cv656
     DF4C DF52     
11358               cv657
11359 DF4E C03A  30 	mov *r10+,r0
11360 DF50 0450  20 	b *r0
11361               cv656

11717               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11718               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and
11719               	; 	' taking it while still standing among the things that charged it -- with
11720               	; 	' a second hazard 48 px behind the first -- is how one mistake becomes
11721               	; 	' three. Clearing the row makes the penalty a single event you can walk
11722               	; 	' away from.
11723               	; 	'
11724               	; 	' BOTH SLOTS, WHATEVER IS IN THEM. Radios used to be exempt: they are
11725               	; 	' CHARACTERS stamped into the name table rather than sprites, so zeroing
11726               	; 	' the kind would have stopped them colliding while leaving them plainly
11727               	; 	' visible on the shelf, and a fixture that is still there has to still be
11728               	; 	' there. That was a reason to UNDRAW them, not a reason to keep them --

11906               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11907               	; 	'
11908               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11909               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11910               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11911               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11912               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11913               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11914               	; 	'
11915               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11916               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11917               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.
11918               	; 	'
11919               	; 	' UNSIGNED-SAFE. Riding up is above the shared floor and riding down is
11920               	; 	' below it, which is a signed quantity, and CVBasic's variables are not.
11921               	; 	' So both are collected as POSITIVE heights on opposite sides -- Kelly's
11922               	; 	' climb plus Harry's descent on one side, Harry's climb on the other --
11923               	; 	' and the difference is taken between two numbers that cannot go
11924               	; 	' negative. Two riders passing on the same flight measure the sum of
11925               	; 	' their heights, which is exactly the distance between them.

12031               	; 	' RIDING WITH THE DOORS SHUT: HIDE HIM AND DO NOT DRAW HIM AT ALL.
12032               	; 	'

12034               	; 	' placed him at his old floor and then hid him again. That is not free.
12035               	; 	' CVBasic's SPRITE writes a RAM mirror which the vblank ISR copies to
12036               	; 	' VRAM, so a vblank landing BETWEEN the draw and the hide latches the
12037               	; 	' visible state for a frame -- and draw_actors is long (Kelly, Harry,
12038               	; 	' eight obstacles) while a pass on the lift screen spans two or three
12039               	; 	' frames, so it happened constantly. He flickered at the floor he had
12040               	; 	' just left, which reads as a drawing bug rather than as a journey.
12041               	; 	'
12042               	; 	' Deciding BEFORE drawing costs one test and cannot race the ISR at all:
12043               	; 	' the mirror never holds a position to be caught with.

12255               	; 		' divide -- `/` compiles to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and
12256               	; 		' this is per-frame code. Two adjacent bits give 0,4,8,12.

13094               	;
13095               	; 	' ======================================================================
13096               	; 	' THE SCANNER
13097               	; 	' ======================================================================
13098               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13099               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13100               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13101               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13102               	; 	'
13103               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13104               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13105               	; 	'
13106               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13107               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13108               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13109               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13110               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13111               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight

13115               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so

13142               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13143               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13144               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13145               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13146               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13147               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13148               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13149               	; 	'
13150               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13151               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13152               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13153               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13154               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13155               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13156               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13171               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13172               	; 	'
13173               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13174               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13175               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13176               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13177               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13178               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13179               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13180               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13181               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13182               	; 	'
13183               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13184               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13185               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13186               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13187               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13188               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13189               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13190               	; 	'
13191               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13192               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13193               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13194               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13195               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13196               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13197               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13198               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13199               	; 	' with room to spare.
13200               	; 	'
13201               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13202               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13203               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13204               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13205               	; 	WAIT
13206               	; 	#endif
13207               	; 	' ONLY THE CELLS THAT MOVE, AND ONLY THIS SCREEN'S. genart.py measures
13208               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13209               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13210               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13211               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13212               	; 	'
13213               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13214               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13215               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13216               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13217               	; 	'
13218               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO
13219               	; 	' flights: floor 1's crosses into a shop floor and floor 3's into the
13220               	; 	' roof, so it needed both composite sets -- nine characters against the
13221               	; 	' east's six, 216 bytes a pass against 144. It measured 20 passes a
13222               	; 	' second where the east screen managed 24-26. The two sets are

13527               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is

13529               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say

13534               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries

13536               	; 	'

13825               	;
13826               	; scan_or1:
13827               cvb_SCAN_OR1
13828               	; 	' THE ONE READ-MODIFY-WRITE ON THE PATTERN TABLE. The radar ORs a
13829               	; 	' pixel row into a canvas character, so it has to know what is already
13830               	; 	' there. On the NES that read comes from nsc, which scan_wipe zeroed
13831               	; 	' and which only this routine writes -- so it is exact, not an
13832               	; 	' approximation of what the PPU holds.
13833               	; 	' AND ON THE NES IT CLEARS RATHER THAN SETS, WHICH IS NOT A TYPO.
13834               	; 	'
13835               	; 	' This routine only ever draws the escalator flights (three call sites,
13836               	; 	' all in scan_escs). On the TI they are drawn as INK and coloured black by
13837               	; 	' scan_escc, so the bits go IN. Here the canvas is wiped to green -- plane
13838               	; 	' 0 set everywhere, see scan_wipe -- and black is index 0, so the flight
13839               	; 	' is made by taking plane 0 bits OUT. Same pixels, opposite sense.
13840               	; 	'
13841               	; 	' 255 - fm1 is NOT fm1: a byte subtracted from all-ones never borrows, so
13842               	; 	' it is the bitwise complement without needing one.
13843               	; 	#if NES
13844               	; 	#nsi = #sda - #nsb
13845               	; 	sva = nsc(#nsi)
13846               	; 	fmn = 255 - fm1
13847               	; 	sva = sva AND fmn
13848               	; 	nsc(#nsi) = sva
13849               	; 	#else

13943               	;
13944               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
13945               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
13946               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
13947               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
13948               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
13949               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
13950               	; scan_wipe:
13951               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
13952               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
13953               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
13954               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
13955               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
13956               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
13957               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
13958               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
13959               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
13960               	; 	'
13961               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
13962               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
13963               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
13964               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
13965               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
13966               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
13967               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
13968               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
13969               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
13970               	; 	'
13971               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
13972               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
13973               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
13974               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
13975               	; 	'
13976               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
13977               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
13978               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns

13983               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that

14001               	; 	' TWELVE BURSTS, NOT SIX: 48 tiles of SIXTEEN bytes. The shadow is indexed
14002               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
14003               	; 	' half of what it holds is the second bitplane, which this port never sets
14004               	; 	' and scan_or1 therefore never reads as ink.
14005               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
14006               	; 	'
14007               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
14008               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
14009               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
14010               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
14011               	; 	'
14012               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
14013               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
14014               	; 	' plane 0 to reach index 0 (the backdrop, black) -- see scan_or1, which
14015               	; 	' is why it ANDs here and ORs on the TI. Writing zeros here instead would
14016               	; 	' leave the instrument black-on-black and the flights invisible.
14017               	; 	'
14018               	; 	' A tile is sixteen bytes: 0-7 are plane 0 and 8-15 plane 1, so the byte's
14019               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
14020               	; 	' AND THE MARGINS ARE GREY, WHICH IS THE OTHER BITPLANE PAIR.
14021               	; 	'
14022               	; 	' The canvas is three character rows -- 24 pixel rows -- of which the
14023               	; 	' instrument uses the middle SIXTEEN (rows 4-19: four levels of four).
14024               	; 	' The outer eight are deliberate air, four above and four below, so the
14025               	; 	' radar does not butt against the shop floor above it or the screen edge
14026               	; 	' below. On the TI those rows take the scanner's own background; here they
14027               	; 	' are index 2, the store's grey, against the instrument's green.
14028               	; 	'
14029               	; 	' Two bitplanes give the four colours this canvas needs and nothing else
14030               	; 	' has to change: index 1 green is plane 0, index 2 grey is plane 1, and
14031               	; 	' the floor lines and flights work on top of those (scan_furn, scan_or1).
14032               	; 	'
14033               	; 	' The byte's place in the canvas says which it is. 256 bytes is one
14034               	; 	' CHARACTER row (16 tiles of 16), the low three bits are the pixel row
14035               	; 	' within the tile, and bit 3 of the position picks the bitplane.

14560               	;
14561               	; #if NES
14562               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14563               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14564               	; 	' screen different colours.
14565               	; 	'
14566               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14567               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14568               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14569               	; 	'
14570               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14571               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14572               	; 	'
14573               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14574               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14575               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14576               	; 	'
14577               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14578               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14579               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14580               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14581               	; 	'
14582               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14583               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot

14587               	; 	' $55, NOT $50 -- ALL FOUR QUADRANTS ON P1, not just the bottom two.
14588               	; 	'
14589               	; 	' $50 put the HUD's own row (name row 2) on P1 and left rows 0-1 on P0.
14590               	; 	' That was invisible while text sat on the backdrop, and stopped being so
14591               	; 	' the moment the font gained a PAPER: rows 0-1 are blank cells, and a blank
14592               	; 	' cell is all paper, so they came out in P0's index 1 -- the store's GREEN
14593               	; 	' -- as a green band above the score line. Nothing is drawn up there, so
14594               	; 	' putting the whole byte on P1 costs nothing and the HUD reads as one band

15071               	;
15072               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15073               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15074               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15075               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15076               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15077               	; 	'
15078               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15079               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15080               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15081               	; 	'
15082               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15083               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15084               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15085               	; 	'
15086               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15087               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15088               	; 	'
15089               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15090               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15091               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15092               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15093               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15094               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15095               	; 	'
15096               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15097               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15098               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15099               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15100               	; 	'
15101               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15102               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15103               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in

15221               	;
15222               	; 	' AND IT ENDS ON ITS LAST BLIP -- there is no closing accent.
15223               	; 	'
15224               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15225               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15226               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15227               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15228               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15229               	; 	'
15230               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15231               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15232               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15233               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15234               	; 	' counting stops.
15235               	;
15236               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15237               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15238               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15239               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15240               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15241               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15242               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15243               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15244               	; 	'
15245               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15246               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15247               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15291 F844 F66A     	data cvb_TIME_SHOW
15292               	; 	' THE CAST IS NOT TAKEN AWAY YET -- hide_all now runs AFTER the beat.
15293               	; 	'
15294               	; 	' It used to run here, so the moment the clock emptied, Harry and the
15295               	; 	' thing that had just hit him vanished and the sound played over an empty
15296               	; 	' store. The hit that ENDS a round is the worst case: `do_hit` sets tout
15297               	; 	' before the freeze starts and the main loop leaves on the very next pass,
15298               	; 	' so the hit sound gets one tick and everything is already gone.
15299               	; 	'
15300               	; 	' The pause drains the sound; leaving the actors up means it drains over
15301               	; 	' the picture that caused it. Nothing is moving -- the pause ticks sfx_tick
15302               	; 	' and nothing else -- so it is a held tableau, not a frozen game.
15303               	; 	' THE MESSAGE BOX, ON THE GAME SCREEN AND NOT INSTEAD OF IT.
15304               	; 	'
15305               	; 	' It used to CLS before GAME OVER, so the last thing the player saw was
15306               	; 	' the store being deleted and then two words on an empty field -- which
15307               	; 	' reads as the program ending rather than as the game ending. The store
15308               	; 	' stays; the message sits in the middle of it.
15309               	; 	'
15310               	; 	' THE BOX IS THE FONT'S OWN BACKGROUND. Every font character is black on
15311               	; 	' HUD_BG (dark blue), so a row of SPACES is a solid dark blue bar. A blank
15312               	; 	' row above and below the text is a frame for the price of two strings and
15313               	; 	' no new characters, and it reads against the store because nothing else on
15314               	; 	' the playfield is that colour.
15315               	; 	'
15316               	; 	' THIRTEEN WIDE, WHICH IS THE LONGEST MESSAGE PLUS ONE EITHER SIDE.
15317               	; 	' HE GOT AWAY and THE BIPLANE are both eleven. Every string below is padded
15318               	; 	' to exactly thirteen so the box has straight edges, and column 10 puts it
15319               	; 	' at columns 10-22 -- centre 16, the screen's.
15320               	; 	'
15321               	; 	' THE REASON IS ALWAYS ON THE SAME ROW, and that is what lets one layout
15322               	; 	' serve both cases. Losing a life draws three rows around it; losing the
15323               	; 	' last one draws two more ON TOP, so GAME OVER appears above the reason
15324               	; 	' rather than replacing it. Printing the reason at a different row for each
15325               	; 	' case would need `PRINT AT` with a variable, and every other PRINT in this
15326               	; 	' program uses a constant.
15327               	; 	#if NES
15328               	; 	' FLUSH THE PASS BEFORE DRAWING A BOX. PPUBUF accumulates for a whole loop
15329               	; 	' pass and is emptied by one NMI, so a message box -- sixty-four cells,
15330               	; 	' sixty-four single-byte descriptors -- was landing in the same vblank as
15331               	; 	' every radar poke and HUD digit the pass had made. The copy then ran past
15332               	; 	' the end of vblank and the tail was DISCARDED at the PPU: a box with
15333               	; 	' characters missing, and the cut moving from run to run, which is why it

15599               	;
15600               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15601               	; 	'
15602               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15603               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15604               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15605               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15606               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15607               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15608               	; 	'
15609               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15610               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15611               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15612               	; 	'
15613               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15614               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15615               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15616               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15617               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15618               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15619               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15620               	; 	'
15621               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15622               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15623               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15624               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15625               	; 	'
15626               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15627               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15628               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15629               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15630               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15631               	; 	'
15632               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15633               	; 	' did not finish.
15634               	; pause_beat:
15635               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT

15699               	; 	' A HIT FALLS -- testsounds variant 5B. Five steps down, 666 -> 411 -> 294
15700               	; 	' -> 235 -> 188 Hz, fading 13 -> 10 as it goes.
15701               	; 	'
15702               	; 	' It was ONE held tone at divisor 900 (124 Hz), which said "something
15703               	; 	' happened" and nothing else. A fall is the mirror of the prize arpeggio's
15704               	; 	' rise, and that pairing is the point: the two events the player causes are
15705               	; 	' now a descent and an ascent, distinguishable with eyes shut.
15706               	; 	'
15707               	; 	' shf marks WHICH channel-1 effect is playing. sht is the shared note-off
15708               	; 	' timer for this channel and `sfe` uses it too, for a single held tone --

15996               cv967
15997               	;
15998               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
15999               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16000               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16001               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16002               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16003               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16004               	;
16005               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16006               	; 	'
16007               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16008               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16009               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16010               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16011               	; 	'
16012               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16013               	; 	'
16014               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16015               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16016               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16017               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16018               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16019               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16020               	; 	'
16021               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16022               	; 	'
16023               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16024               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16025               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16026               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16027               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16028               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16029               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16030               	; 	'
16031               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16032               	; 	'
16033               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16034               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16035               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16036               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16037               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16038               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16039               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16040               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16041               	; 	'
16042               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16043               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16044               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16045               	; 	'
16046               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16047               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16048               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16049               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16050               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16051               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16052               	; 	'
16053               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16054               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16055               	; 	'
16056               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16057               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16058               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16059               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16060               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16061               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16062               	; 	'
16063               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16064               	; 	'
16065               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16066               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16067               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16068               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand

16270               	;
16271               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16272               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16273               	; 	'
16274               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16275               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16276               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16277               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16278               	; 	'
16279               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16280               	; 	'
16281               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16282               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16283               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16284               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16285               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16286               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16287               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16288               	; 	'
16289               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16290               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16291               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16292               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16293               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16294               	; 	'
16295               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16296               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16297               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16298               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16299               	; 	#if TI994A
16300               	; 	BANK 2
16301      01EC     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

16775               	; 	' AND THE TITLE'S DISPLAY LIST, for the same reason as the font: walked
16776               	; 	' once by title_draw, at boot and on a return to the title, and never
16777               	; 	' during play. title_draw selects bank 2 around its walk.
16778               	; 	'
16779               	; 	' ITS MESSAGE BOXES DID NOT COME WITH IT. They are the same format and
16780               	; 	' were in the same generated file, which is what made this worth doing
16781               	; 	' carefully: they are walked when a ROUND ENDS, mid-game, so on bank 2
16782               	; 	' they would have returned bytes from the wrong page at the moment a life
16783               	; 	' is lost -- and with no error at build or run time. gentitle.py now
16784               	; 	' writes them to title.bas below, which stays in bank 1.
16785               	; 	INCLUDE "titledl.bas"
16786               	; 	' ==================================================
16787               	; 	' THE TITLE SCREEN, AS A DISPLAY LIST
16788               	; 	' Generated by assets/gentitle.py -- do not edit here.
16789               	; 	'
16790               	; 	' row, col, length, then `length` bytes; 255 ends.
16791               	; 	' Walked by title_draw only.
16792               	; 	'
16793               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2, with the fonts, because it is read ONCE
16794               	; 	' -- at boot and on a return to the title. title_draw
16795               	; 	' selects bank 2 around its walk and restores bank 1.
16796               	; 	' The message boxes in title.bas are the same format and
16797               	; 	' CANNOT come with it: they are read when a round ends.
16798               	; 	' ==================================================
16799               	;
16800               	; title_tbl:
16801               cvb_TITLE_TBL
